items.author: gregisenberg
items.name: GREG ISENBERG
items.text:
I just got back from SF and I FEEL INSPIRED.

I spent 5 days with frontier AI model teams, AI startup founders, and 3 billionaires. 

My takeaways:

1. I had lunch with 3 billionaires. All of them are buying SaaS companies and rebuilding them agent-first. They were deeply inspired by Bending Spoons and Ryan Cohen's eBay deal. Buy the company, cut the headcount, rebuild the tech, add agents, add features, make more valuable experience, raise prices.

2. The frontier model companies are hungry for usage data from the field. They can see API calls and token counts. They can't see the actual workflows. If you're deep in a niche using these models in ways the model companies haven't seen, that understanding is incredibly valuable. Usage intelligence is the new alpha.

3. Consumer AI is massively underbuilt. Every billboard in SF is either B2B inference infrastructure or vertical agent companies. The entire city is optimized for enterprise. Meanwhile you have companies like Cal AI  doing $50M ARR in 18 months as a consumer app. I met with a cool few teams doing consumer AI (@paulscherer  / @ekuyda) 

4. MCP came up in literally every conversation. The companies exposing their product as MCP endpoints are getting pulled into deals they never pitched for. The ones that aren't are becoming invisible to agents. This is the new SEO. If agents can't find you, you don't exist. Building products for agents is the new zeitgeist in general.

5. Not uncommon for hot seed rounds to be $25-50  million valuations. I saw a Series A at $450 million

6. If I had a dollar every time someone mentioned "forward-deployed engineer" this trip I could have funded a seed round. It's the hottest role in SF right now. The person who sits between the agent and the customer, making sure everything actually works.

7. The mood around open source shifted. A year ago it felt like open source was chasing the frontier models. Now founders are telling me Gemma and DeepSeek are good enough for 80% of what they need at a fraction of the cost. The "which model do you use" conversation is being replaced by "which model for which task." Model loyalty kinda feels dead.

8. Voice agents came up more than I expected. Multiple founders told me voice is the interface for the next billion users. The billion people who will never type a prompt will absolutely talk to one.

9. The Obsidian community in SF is weirdly intense. Multiple founders showed me their vaults unprompted. Like showing someone your home gym. It's a flex now. The quality of your knowledge base (second brain?)  is becoming a status symbol among builders.

10. Maybe it was just the people I met but the age of the founders is shifting. I met more founders over 40 this trip than any trip before and more founders under age 21 than ever before. Founders getting older and younger at the same time.

11. I spoke to a lot of fast-growing startups, VCs and frontier models who are hiring content creators right now. 

12. The restaurant scene in SF is actually better than it's been in years. Founders are going out more. Alcohol is out, not surprisingly. 

13. SF doesn't feel like the only place anymore. We all have access to the same frontier models. We all read the same X feed. A founder in NYC or Lagos is calling the same APIs as a founder in SoMa. So in the past it felt like SF was always lightyears ahead, doesn't feel that way anymore. It's okay not to live in SF and have BIG DREAMS.

14. The coworking spaces in SF are half empty but the coffee shops are packed. People want to be around people. I had a few startup ideas here....

15. Walking around the Mission I noticed something: the street-level businesses, the taquerias, the barbershops, the laundromats, none of them use any AI at all. 

16. I heard the phrase "agent debt" for the first time. Like technical debt but for agents. When you hack together an agent workflow fast and never clean it up, the system prompts conflict, the memory gets polluted, the tools overlap. 6 months later the agent is doing weird things and nobody knows why lol. 

17. Met a few people who carry two phones now. One for personal. One that's basically an agent terminal running Telegram or iMessage connections to their agent fleet.

It's always amazing to get that dose of inspiration in SF. I FEEL INSPIRED.

But I'm so happy to be back home, locked in and building. 

We're 12-18 months into a shift that will take 15 years to play out. The urgency in every conversation was real.

What an incredible time to be building.

items.author: levie
items.name: Aaron Levie
items.text:
Great post on FDEs. Everyone should read it if you’re interested in this job category. This is a job that is going to be around as long as AI keeps changing rapidly, which it inevitably will. 

People often wonder why isn’t this like just deploying other forms of technology in the past, like cloud. 

Because something like cloud adoption affected a fairly concentrated set of users (developers and IT), and generally didn’t require a fundamental change to the workflows of employees to get the benefits of the new service being delivered on the cloud. At best you went to one training session and you were done. 

With agents, the work to implement them is not only highly technical, but they directly impact the underlying workflows that people participate in. This means there’s a ton of technical work and change management that comes with it.

Further, the pace of change of cloud wasn’t nearly as quick, so there was a lot more time for best practices to propagate. Now, every model change means either something new can be done that wasn’t possible before, or some piece of scaffolding is now redundant or holding you back. 

This is why it’s commonly easier for a vendor or partner that’s seen the implementation hundreds or thousands of times help do the work, even with internal support from the customer.

So, this job isn’t going away any time soon, and will be a great path for a lot of technical talent, especially early career.

items.title: Debarghya Das — SF wealth divide essay
items.author: deedydas
items.name: Deedy
items.text:
The vibes in SF feel pretty frenetic right now. The divide in outcomes is the worst I've ever seen.

Over the last 5yrs, a group of ~10k people - employees at Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Nvidia, Meta TBD, founders - have hit retirement wealth of well above $20M (back of the envelope AI estimation).

Everyone outside that group feels like they can work their well-paying (but <$500k) job for their whole life and never get there.

Worse yet, layoffs are in full swing. Many software engineers feel like their life's skill is no longer useful. The day to day role of most jobs has changed overnight with AI.

As a result,
1. The corporate ladder looks like the wrong building to climb.
Everyone's trying to align with a new set of career "paths": should I be a founder? Is it too late to join Anthropic / OpenAI? should I get into AI? what company stock will 10x next? People are demanding higher salaries and switching jobs more and more.

2. There’s a deep malaise about work (and its future).
Why even work at all for “peanuts”? Will my job even exist in a few years? Many feel helpless. You hear the “permanent underclass” conversation a lot, esp from young people. It's hard to focus on doing good work when you think "man, if I joined Anthropic 2yrs ago, I could retire"

3. The mid to late middle managers feel paralyzed.
Many have families and don't feel like they have the energy or network to just "start a company". They don't particularly have any AI skills. They see the writing on the wall: middle management is being hollowed out in many companies.

4. The rich aren’t particularly happy either.
No one is shedding tears for them (and rightfully so). But those who have "made it" experience a profound lack of purpose too. Some have gone from <$150k to >$50M in a few years with no ramp. It flips your life plans upside down. For some, comparison is the thief of joy. For some, they escape to NYC to "live life". For others still, they start companies "just cuz", often to win status points. They never imagined that by age 30, they'd be set. I once asked a post-economic founder friend why they didn't just sell the co and they said "and do what? right now, everyone wants to talk to me. if i sell, I will only have money."

I understand that many reading this scoff at the champagne problems of the valley. Society is warped in this tech bubble. What is often well-off anywhere else in the world is bang average here.

Unlike many other places, tenure, intelligence and hard work can be loosely correlated with outcomes in the Bay. Living through a societally transformative gold rush in that environment can be paralyzing. "Am I in the right place? Should I move? Is there time still left? Am I gonna make it?" It psychologically torments many who have moved here in search of "success".

Ironically, a frequent side effect of this torment is to spin up the very products making everyone rich in hopes that you too can vibecode your path to economic enlightenment.

 3. Agents layer: this layers made of agents (multi /specialised)

items.author: GeniusGTX
items.name: GeniusThinking
items.text:
Marc Andreessen just revealed how Harvard Business School was built on a broken 1941 theory, and how it's now collapsing...

Andreessen co-founded Netscape in 1994 and a16z in 2009.

He has sat on Meta's board since 2008.

He has spent 30 years backing founders and watching managerial CEOs lose to them.

The pattern traces back to one book: James Burnham's *The Machiavellians* (1941).

Burnham argued every great company had been founder-run.

Henry Ford ran Ford. Bob Noyce ran Intel.

Today, Elon Musk runs Tesla, SpaceX, and Starlink.

Then, he said, something broke.

Between the 1880s and the 1920s, a new philosophy replaced the founder. It was called managerialism.

The professional manager would now hold a portable skill, usable across any business.

The consequences were:

- Harvard Business School
- Stanford Business School
- Management as a universal skill

items.name: Boring_Business
items.text:
Probably the best take I have heard on why there is so much fear around software exposure in private equity and credit because of AI

From David Sacks

"Historically we only had two good exits for software businesses. One was IPO. The other was M&A. Then these big private equity shops came along and gave us a third potential exit. You would sell to them and then they would raise the capital based on one third equity and two third debt. So it was debt financed buyouts. 

It is something that has been around in the non technology part of the economy for a long time but was a relatively new entrant in the world of technology. And the reason for that is if you have debt financed a purchase, you need to have very stable cash flows. 

Because if you miss and you cant pay your interest on the debt, you will lose all your equity because the debt holders will foreclose. 

It was belief for a long time that software did have predictable cash flows, at least for the mature businesses."

items.title: @heynavtoor — Claude job-application pipeline (open source)
items.author: heynavtoor
items.name: Nav Toor
items.text:
A scientist in Denmark figured out how to make Claude prepare his job applications. He open-sourced the whole thing.

His name is Mads Lorentzen. He is a PhD geophysicist. He built it on top of Claude Code and released it under MIT license.

Here is what it does. You fork the repo, fill in your background once, and it runs a five-step pipeline for every job you want to apply to.

Step 1. It reads the job posting and scores how well you fit.

Step 2. It drafts a tailored CV in LaTeX, picking only the experience that matches.

Step 3. It writes a cover letter framed around what you would bring to the role.

Step 4. A second AI agent reviews the first agent's work, points out weaknesses, and the first agent revises.

Step 5. It compiles both into clean PDFs you can send.

The whole thing is a folder of markdown files. The candidate profile, the writing style rules, the CV templates, the interview prep notes. Every step is plain text you can read and change.

The job portal search is built for Danish boards. The application workflow itself works for any country.

489 stars. 270 forks. A fork-to-star ratio that high means people are using it, not only bookmarking.

Mads is not a startup founder. He built this because he needed it for himself, then shared it.

This is the future of job hunting. Not a service you pay for. A workflow you own.

(Link in the comments)

items.author: gabriell_lab
items.name: Gabriel

media.description: A side-by-side A/B demo of the tip. Two identical 'Acme™' mobile-app mockups sit next to each other — the left labeled 'Velocity Stretch + Motion Blur', the right 'Static Shape + No Blur'. As the active-tab indicator dot animates between the nav items (Home / Feed / Explore / Activity), the left version stretches and motion-blurs the moving element in its direction of travel before settling, while the right one moves rigidly with no deformation — demonstrating how velocity-driven squash/stretch makes the exact same transition feel far more dynamic.

media.description: A screen recording of mymind's new Vibe Search on the app's signature vivid orange-red backdrop. It opens in the card library (an editorial italic-serif 'images' search with tabs for Images / Screenshots / Snippets / Web Pages / Movies / Books / Articles / Notes over a masonry grid of colour blocks), then focuses the search field — the mymind sun/spiral mark beside a giant italic-serif 'Describe your…' placeholder — and finally runs the natural-language query 'mid century wooden furniture,' returning a semantic mood board of saved cards: a bent-plywood lounge chair, a green sofa in a wood-panelled room, a saved Product (a mid-century rattan glass coffee table tagged $312.49) and warm-lit interiors. items.text:
Introducing, VIBE SEARCH (Beta).

The search in mymind has always been more focused on fast, specific and accurate recall.

Our regular search is incredibly fast, with instant results as you type and it gives you a lot of tools for engaging in deep searches (like drilling into a category, time travel searches, OCR etc.). It works really well for recalling and finding specific things.

The new Vibe Search mode is a bit different and more semantic in nature. It's great for when you want to search for "a vibe or a feeling" and in return get back more of a mood board of results instead of one specific one.

The new Vibe Search is similar to our Same Vibe feature, the only difference is that you drive it with your own words. You can be as specific as you want, and the larger your personal library is, the better it gets. I use it almost daily now for various use cases.

PS: The new Vibe Search does not just include images, but also other cards you saved to your mind, such as Websites, Products or Notes. The Vibe Search understands your context based on how you phrase your query and gives you results based on that.

PPS: This feature is currently hidden behind the Research Lab toggle (via settings) and available on both the web app and MacOS app.

June 2023: first ever demo we made of what ended up becoming Dot and its "zoomy view"

I've made many things that have been called "early"… Mercury, MakeSpace, Dot… and what I can share is that there's no magic in "early." We never once tried to be early! Our goal has always been to make things that are true, and I believe truth is something you feel before you can prove.

I've learned that my job as founder is to protect the process long enough for "true" to become "on time." And we're almost ready to share...

If you're an exceptional engineer or operator who wants to build what's true before it's obvious, you know where to find me.

More soon,

items.title: Stagger grid reveal — a Motion.dev design-engineering tip
items.author: gabriell_lab
items.name: Gabriel

media.description: A screen recording of an 8-card image grid (moody stock photos like 'Full Gas', 'Whiteout', 'White Monolith', 'Golden Hour') with a 'Reveal / Hide' toggle and a 'Swing' button above it; clicking Hide then Reveal re-triggers each card fading/sliding in with a small per-card stagger delay and a subtle rotational swing, demonstrating the Motion.dev `stagger()` code snippet from the tweet.

items.text:
Design Engineering Tip:

Don’t reveal a grid all at once.
Use stagger() to give every item a tiny delay.
You can add an extra motion detail to give the reveal more character, like this tiny swing.

import { stagger } from "motion"

animateView(update)
  .add(".item")
  .enter(
    { opacity: [0, 1], y: [12, 0], rotate: [-2, 0] },
    { delay: stagger(0.05, { from: "center" }) }
  )

_schema.note: Per-site design teardowns extracted live via Playwright MCP (fullPage screenshot + hover + scroll + a mandatory DOM probe + a mobile resize). Keyed by domain. Prose-forward: prose describes what the site IS/shows/does; a structured sidecar (from the DOM probe) makes tokens queryable. Color/font claims come from the DOM (getComputedStyle/document.fonts/CSS vars), never from eyeballing the screenshot.

fields.screenshot: saved fullPage PNG of the main view
fields.extracted_via: tool + viewport(s); includes logged_out:true when viewed without auth
fields.what_it_is: prose: what the site is and what it's for
fields.what_it_shows: prose: the content actually on screen
fields.how_it_works: prose: navigation, interaction, scroll/hover behavior, the flow of the experience
fields.how_its_designed: prose: layout, typography, motion, imagery medium, the craft and the choices behind it

fields.tech_stack: string[]: framework + analytics + host detected from DOM/scripts

weirdfolders.com.title: Weird Folders — Custom Folder Icons for Mac & PC
weirdfolders.com.tagline: Custom Folder Icons for your Operative System, download a free pack or learn to make them yourself
weirdfolders.com.what_it_is: A freemium storefront selling custom folder icons for Mac and PC, disguised as a playful collection you browse. There's no marketing preamble — you land directly inside the product. The whole pitch is 'here are ~100 weird little folder icons; pick a few free, or buy the full pack for €9.'
weirdfolders.com.what_it_shows: A single fixed screen packed edge-to-edge with a dense grid of folder icons, each a tiny tactile render of an everyday object — a Green G-Shock, a Pizza Box, a VHS tape, Cheetos, a fish bowl, Marlboros, an iPod, a hard disk. The product literally IS the page. Chrome is minimal: a small top-left 'Weird Folders' wordmark, an Awwwards 'Honors' badge, and a bottom bar holding the buy CTA plus a 'Pick 5 icons → free pack' progress nudge.
weirdfolders.com.how_it_works: The grid is a pannable/draggable infinite canvas — you move around the collection spatially rather than scrolling a page (body scroll is disabled). Every icon is a clickable button; clicking selects toward the free-pack unlock. A S/M/L switcher rescales grid density (M by default), acting like a zoom control. Primary action is 'Buy Full Pack — €9'; secondary paths are the gamified 'Pick 5 → free pack' and 'Register to get a free pack.' On load, an interstitial modal interrupts with the Awwwards Honors nomination and a 'Vote for us →' link.
weirdfolders.com.how_its_designed: A near-black ground makes the colorful icon renders pop like objects laid out on a dark table — the page is all product, no decoration. Icons are drawn on ~99 individual elements (not ), giving them a crisp, almost 3D product-shot quality and enabling per-icon hover/scale animation (transitions/transforms run heavy across the page). Typography is deliberately quiet so the icons carry the personality: Inter Tight for all UI text, with Fraunces serif reserved for accent headings like the modal title (24px, semibold, slightly tightened tracking). Built on Tailwind + shadcn; tellingly, the underlying design-token system is actually a warm cream/stone LIGHT palette, deliberately overridden to near-black for this gallery view.
weirdfolders.com.palette: Near-black ground (#131211 / #252422), warm off-white text (#edebe8), muted taupe for secondary (#9f9a93); all real color comes from the per-icon renders, plus a light pill for the buy CTA.

chusmargallo.space.title: Chus Margallo Portfolio | Interactive Desktop Experience
chusmargallo.space.tagline: A retro operating system-inspired portfolio. Explore projects and experience a unique web-based desktop interface.
chusmargallo.space.what_it_is: A portfolio for designer Chus Margallo built as a fully interactive retro operating system. Instead of a scrolling page, the site boots you into a fake desktop OS where the work lives inside windows, folders, and clickable desktop icons.
chusmargallo.space.what_it_shows: A pixel-art desktop: a vivid 8-bit ocean-wave/beach wallpaper (palm tree, breaking wave) filling the screen, a classic top menu bar ('Chus.exe' · File / Edit / View / Window / Help with a clock top-right), a column of labelled desktop icons down the left (My Work, About, Trash…), and a bottom dock. A cookie-policy notice appears as a system dialog window sitting on the desktop.
chusmargallo.space.how_it_works: A desktop metaphor, not a webpage — the viewport is fixed (body overflow:hidden, nothing scrolls); you navigate by clicking desktop icons and menu-bar items to open windows. Interaction is OS-style: open, drag, close. The ~18 buttons stand in for files and apps, so movement through the portfolio is spatial and skeuomorphic rather than linear.
chusmargallo.space.how_its_designed: Wall-to-wall retro-computing nostalgia, rendered entirely in the Silkscreen pixel font over clean near-white system chrome. The centerpiece is a hand-pixelled beach scene that reads like a CRT desktop wallpaper, and every UI element commits to the bit — menu bar, dialogs, dock and iconography all mimic a vintage GUI. Visuals are raster pixel-art sprites (~25 , no canvas or video), which keeps the whole thing feeling like a real old operating system rather than a slick modern site.
chusmargallo.space.palette: Near-white system chrome (#fafafa / #fff), dark slate text (#0f1729) with muted slate secondary (#65758b); all the saturated color comes from the pixel-art beach wallpaper.

daviskeene.com.title: Home | Davis Keene
daviskeene.com.tagline: Davis Keene's personal website — engineer, software developer, creator
daviskeene.com.what_it_is: The personal homepage of Davis Keene, an engineer at Handshake. A deliberately minimal, text-first 'about me' page that he's been incrementally making 'more fun' with small interactive flourishes (the subject of his 'making my personal site more fun' posts).
daviskeene.com.what_it_shows: A centered single column on near-white. Up top: a geometric 'K' monogram (two black triangles) with a slim nav — More / Projects / Photos / Blog — and a moon icon for dark mode. Below it, a black-and-white self-portrait sliced into offset, scattered rectangles (a glitchy photo-collage effect), then a warm first-person intro: 'Happy Thursday! I'm Davis, an engineer, software developer, creator, twin, illini, rock climber, coffee drinker…' with inline underlined links to Handshake, UIUC and a résumé. Footer is three social glyphs (Twitter, GitHub, LinkedIn).
daviskeene.com.how_it_works: A plain vertical page you read top-to-bottom; navigate via the underlined inline links or the top nav to Projects / Photos / Blog. The main interactive control is a light/dark theme toggle (moon icon). The personality lives in micro-interactions — chiefly the fragmented portrait — rather than in heavy motion or layout tricks; it's the 'fun' experiment grafted onto an otherwise classic résumé page.
daviskeene.com.how_its_designed: Restrained editorial minimalism: generous whitespace, a single centered measure of text set in Libre Franklin, near-black on off-white. No decorative color, almost no chrome — the lone visual play is the sliced grayscale self-portrait, which gives a standard personal page a quirky, hand-made feel. Tiny footprint (4 images, a handful of SVG social icons, one button), no canvas or video.
daviskeene.com.palette: Off-white ground (#fafafa), near-black text (#000) with grey secondary (#666) — essentially monochrome, plus a dark-mode variant via the toggle.

ditther.com.title: Ditther — Browser-based Image Editor with Dither Effects
ditther.com.what_it_is: A free, no-account browser image editor built around retro/cinematic effects — dither, halftone, bayer matrix, lego, pixel, plus film-style color filters. You drop in an image (or pick a generated background) and restyle it live in the browser.
ditther.com.what_it_shows: A dark single-screen app. The center is a large canvas workspace ('Choose any image to get started') flanked by a right-hand control panel of Effects, Filters and color Tone sliders (Brightness, Contrast, Saturate, Hue, Grayscale, Sepia). A top bar holds Shuffle / Backgrounds / Remix / Upload image / Download; a small changelog card sits bottom-left. Filter presets read like film stocks: Noir, Neon, Golden Hour, Moonlight, Dusted, Dreamy, Cinematic.
ditther.com.how_it_works: It's a real-time editing tool, not a marketing page — ~24 input sliders and ~30 buttons drive a live <canvas> preview. You upload or drag-and-drop an image (or paste), pick an effect/filter, tune the sliders, and Download. No scroll; everything is one workspace. Mode and Blending-Mode dropdowns plus Size/Spread/Amount/Exposure/Scatter/Opacity give fine control over the dithering.
ditther.com.how_its_designed: Confident dark-app aesthetic: near-black panels (#0d0d0f / #141417) with crisp off-white text and a single mint-teal accent (rgb(58,237,201)) for active states. Type is all Geist + Geist Mono, which gives it a clean technical/tool feel. Effect thumbnails preview each look. The restraint (one accent, monospace labels, dense but tidy controls) makes a playful toy read as a serious utility.
ditther.com.palette: Near-black panels (#0d0d0f / #141417), off-white text (#f8f8f8), muted grey labels (#8d8d95), single mint-teal accent (#3aedc9).

12matcha.com.title: 12 Matcha — Forever in Pursuit of Exquisite Matcha
12matcha.com.what_it_is: The brand and commerce site for 12 Matcha, a matcha and dessert boutique in NoHo, New York. It's a refined direct-to-consumer storefront that leads with mood and craft rather than products — the matcha equivalent of a fashion house homepage.
12matcha.com.what_it_shows: A full-bleed photographic hero of an elegant white European-style storefront, overlaid with a centered serif wordmark '12' and the line 'ALWAYS IN PURSUIT'. A minimal top nav (THE 12 APPROACH, THE 12 STORE) and a privacy/cookie banner. Scrolling down (the page is ~4,650px tall) moves through brand story, video, and store sections.
12matcha.com.how_it_works: A long, vertical, scroll-driven brand narrative — full-screen photographic and video sections (5 videos) you move through top to bottom, ending in the store. Navigation is sparse and editorial; the experience is about scrolling through atmosphere before you reach commerce. Includes an accessibility menu and a full cookie-consent customiser.
12matcha.com.how_its_designed: Quiet luxury editorial: a near-white/cream and black palette lets large architectural photography carry the page. The display face is a distinctive monospace-serif ('gc16') used for the big 'ALWAYS IN PURSUIT' headline, paired with abcDiatype as a clean grotesque for body — a fashion-editorial pairing that signals taste and restraint. Generous negative space, centered composition, almost no UI chrome.
12matcha.com.palette: Cream/near-white (#eeede7, #fff) and near-black (#111) with white text over photography; color comes entirely from the imagery.

jessyin.world.title: Jess Yin — hey there
jessyin.world.what_it_is: The personal site of Jess Yin (ex-finance, apparel founder, now building creative web experiences), explicitly styled as a macOS Finder window. It's an about/portfolio hub that frames her life and work inside a familiar desktop-file metaphor.
jessyin.world.what_it_shows: A warm cream canvas with a left sidebar of 'files' (About, Writing, Projects, Say Hi) — the active one highlighted in soft pink — and a reading pane to the right. The About pane is a friendly first-person bio with key phrases (reading, writing, podcasts, SERENA LI, Inseam) highlighted like selected text, closing with X / Substack / TikTok links.
jessyin.world.how_it_works: Navigation mimics a Finder window: click an item in the left sidebar to swap the content pane, rather than loading new pages or scrolling a long document. The viewport is fixed (no page scroll); a single <canvas> adds a subtle ambient touch. Inline highlighted keywords double as links into projects and contact.
jessyin.world.how_its_designed: Soft, tactile, personal: a warm cream ground (#f5f0e8) with rose-pink highlights (#fce4ec / #e8b4bc) and dark grey text, set in the system font for an honest, OS-native feel. The Finder metaphor is the whole concept — sidebar + pane, selection highlights, desktop calm — making a simple bio feel like poking around someone's computer.
jessyin.world.palette: Warm cream ground (#f5f0e8), rose-pink highlights (#fce4ec / #e8b4bc), dark grey text (#333), muted grey secondary (#888).

offthewall.studio.title: Studio Off The Wall
offthewall.studio.what_it_is: The portfolio site of Studio Off The Wall, an independent New Delhi design studio (led by Daniel Lin) that helps brands with how their identity and website 'work, look and feel.' It positions the studio through a curated, magazine-like showcase of project work.
offthewall.studio.what_it_shows: A dense editorial grid on white: stacked project modules ('Simple - things', case-study thumbnails, video stills) around a large serif statement 'Studio Off The Wall' and the tagline 'BORN BY DESIGN, FOR DESIGN'. A labelled header (Studio / Designers: Ashley, Soumitra / What / Get in Touch) and a footer strip with location ('New Delhi, India / World Wide Web') and a live time.
offthewall.studio.how_it_works: A long vertical scroll (~7,360px) through a magazine-style layout of project tiles mixing images and ~10 inline videos. Everything is link-driven (no buttons) — modules open project work; the header and footer carry studio info and contact. It reads like flipping through a printed design annual.
offthewall.studio.how_its_designed: Institutional/archival editorial: crisp white background, a large display serif ('Lastik Free') for statements alongside Times for running text, and a deliberately old-web touch — default blue (#0000ee) hyperlinks — that signals a knowing, type-led sensibility. Strict grid, small labels, lots of metadata; the design language is 'design studio as publication.'
offthewall.studio.palette: White (#fff) and off-white (#f8f8f6) with black text, classic blue links (#0000ee); color comes from project imagery.

gaspardhedde.fr.title: Gaspard Hedde — Creative Developer
gaspardhedde.fr.what_it_is: The portfolio of Gaspard Hedde, a creative developer and Gobelins Paris student who builds websites, apps and immersive experiences. The site is itself a demo of that craft — a minimal frame around an interactive, WebGL-style project showcase.
gaspardhedde.fr.what_it_shows: A pale grey canvas, almost empty by design: a thin 'GASPARD HEDDE' wordmark top-left, social links (CONTACT / LINKEDIN / TWITTER/X / GITHUB) top-right, a fanned 3D-ish stack of colorful project thumbnails floating in the upper right, a 'SNAKE — LIST' view toggle, and a live 'PARIS 17:27:16' clock with a one-line bio bottom-left.
gaspardhedde.fr.how_it_works: A fixed single screen (no scroll, body overflow hidden) where the work lives in an interactive image stack rendered on a <canvas> — you browse projects spatially through the fanned deck, and a SNAKE/LIST toggle switches between the playful stacked view and a plain list. Immersive and motion-led rather than document-like.
gaspardhedde.fr.how_its_designed: Swiss-minimal meets creative-dev showcase: a light grey ground (#f3f3f3), ultra-thin Helvetica (weight 100) for all type, and near-total emptiness so the colorful, slightly glitchy project deck and the ticking Paris clock become the focus. The restraint frames the WebGL interaction as the hero — the layout gets out of the way.
gaspardhedde.fr.palette: Light grey ground (#f3f3f3), black text, white; saturated color only in the project-thumbnail stack.

are.na.title: NOUS RESEARCH / JOHN GALT | Are.na
are.na.tagline: A sample of my work with Nous Research.
are.na.extracted_via: playwright-mcp @ 1440x900 (viewport screenshot; fullPage timed out on the 157-block lazy-loaded grid) + mobile 390x844
are.na.what_it_is: A single channel on Are.na, the research-style bookmarking/moodboard platform. This channel, 'NOUS RESEARCH / JOHN GALT', is curator john-galt's collection — self-described as 'A sample of my work with Nous Research' — and is the source the tweet credits for StudioMilitary's aesthetic.
are.na.what_it_shows: A dense masonry grid of 157 saved blocks: electric-blue dithered/halftone faces, anime and manga portraits, poppy flowers, staff-wielding wizard figures, purple 'HERMES 3' imagery and ritual-poster artwork. A left Info rail lists the description, 'Started over 2 years ago', 'Length 157', 'Followers 18', the channels it appears in (Applied Aesthetics, Brutalist Aesthetics), and a Grid/Table view toggle. The channel is marked CLOSED (read-only) and was viewed logged out.

vivekhaldar.com.what_it_is: A single page from Vivek Haldar's personal “ideaverse” (a knowledge-visualization corner of his site vivekhaldar.com): a D3.js chord diagram titled “Theme Connections,” subtitled “Chord diagram of theme co-occurrence across 321 articles.” It's a self-analytics artifact — he's run his own ~321 blog posts through some theme-extraction pass and is visualizing which pairs of themes tend to appear together in the same piece of writing.
vivekhaldar.com.what_it_shows: A circular chord diagram with 10 colored theme arcs around the ring — AI & LLMs, Programming & Software Engineering, Work Culture & Professional Life, Tools & Technology, Cognitive Science & Learning, Philosophy & Epistemology, Economics & Social Issues, Personal Essays & Culture, Technical Tutorials, and Linguistics & Language — connected by ribbons whose thickness encodes how often two themes co-occur in the same article. AI & LLMs is clearly the fattest arc with the thickest ribbons, dominated by a strong connection to Programming & Software Engineering and a secondary one to Work Culture & Professional Life, while most other themes are linked by thin, low-saturation threads. An empty results panel (“Click a theme arc or chord to see articles”) sits to the right of the diagram.
vivekhaldar.com.how_it_works: Hovering a theme arc (confirmed on “AI & LLMs”) highlights it and pops a small tooltip reading the theme name, its article count (“49 articles”), and “Click to see articles” — clicking presumably filters the side panel to the underlying article list, though that click-through wasn't exercised in this pass. It's built directly on D3 v7 (loaded from the d3js.org CDN) plus a same-origin `articles-data.js` payload — no framework, no build step, no analytics: just a static HTML file, D3, and a JSON-like data file computing and rendering the chord layout client-side.

beatspark.com.fonts: System fonts only (-apple-system, SF Pro Text, Helvetica Neue); no webfont payload

meta.description: Interactive music production lessons inside of Ableton Live.

beatspark.com.responsive_note: At 390px the single screen simply fits the 844px viewport (scrollHeight 844, no overflow); there is no nav to collapse.

palmier.io.title: Palmier Pro | The video editor built for AI
palmier.io.tagline: Palmier Pro is the video editor built for AI.
palmier.io.extracted_via: 1440x900 full-page screenshot + 390x844 DOM pass (no mobile screenshot); Playwright, logged_out: true
palmier.io.what_it_is: Marketing site for Palmier Pro, a non-linear video editor designed to be driven by AI agents such as Claude, Codex and Cursor. palmier.io redirects to www.palmier.io.
palmier.io.what_it_shows: Hero pitch, 'Teach Claude, Codex, Cursor, or your agent how to edit your videos', a single workspace for AI tools, a full NLE feature section, the Palmier Service, an FAQ and a closing download CTA.
palmier.io.how_it_works: A 7,055px page with 2 videos, 52 images and 43 SVGs. Only first-party assets plus the Fontshare API for Satoshi are loaded. Geist and Geist Mono suggest a Next.js-style stack, but the probe found no framework global, so that is not confirmed.
palmier.io.how_its_designed: Warm near-black #0d0c0a with light grey text #ececec, muted #b3b3b3, surfaces #161614 / #1e1e1c, hairline borders (#ffffff12) and a single red accent #e63535. Type is Satoshi for body and headlines (the h1 is 60px at weight 400), Geist Mono for detail and Instrument Serif available for editorial flourishes.
palmier.io.fonts: Satoshi (300-900), Geist, Geist Mono, Instrument Serif

meta.description: Automate repeatable video work with Claude or Codex, generate media on the timeline, and export to your professional editor.
